title: How Scuba Works
summary: Josh and Chuck continue their underwater series with a general overview of scuba diving: the origin of the word and early history (Benoit Rouquayrol and Auguste Denayrouze's 1860s demand regulator and helmet, Christian Lambertsen's LARU rebreather, Jacques Cousteau and Émile Gagnan's Aqua-Lung and The Silent World), types of diving (open water, night, drift, technical, wreck, deep, altitude, cavern and cave, ice), decompression sickness ("the bends") and decompression stops, gear (scuba tank, BCD, regulator, masks, fins, dive computers, wetsuits and drysuits, rebreathers), certification (PADI, NAUI, SSI, Discover Scuba, open water course), risk and fatality statistics, buddy systems, and the safe ascent (SSA/CESA-style controlled emergency swimming ascent). Ends with listener mail correcting kombucha information.

segments.title: Opening banter and underwater series
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open, framing this as a general episode in their underwater series after cave diving, and recall the Scuba Cat episode from the early days.

segments.title: Chuck's snorkeling trip and what scuba stands for
segments.summary: Chuck recounts a snorkeling trip in Mexico where his daughter struggled with the gear and then free-dived happily. They define SCUBA as self-contained underwater breathing apparatus and note that Josh's one open water dive left him seasick.

segments.title: Coral and reef observations
segments.summary: Chuck describes seeing live coral, tropical fish, and artificial PVC reef structures on his trip, and the hosts remark on poor coral condition.

segments.title: Early history: Rouquayrol and Denayrouze's demand regulator
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1860s invention by Benoit Rouquayrol and Auguste Denayrouze of a demand regulator for mine rescue workers, which they then adapted for underwater breathing with a compressed-air backpack, untethered from boats.

segments.title: Early helmets and the Aerophore
segments.summary: Chuck explains early equipment such as lead-soled shoes and a copper helmet with a single window, nicknamed the 'groin' for pig snout, and the Aerophore award at the 1867 World's Fair.

segments.title: Christian Lambertsen and the LARU rebreather
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Christian Lambertsen's 1939 Lambertsen Amphibious Respirator Unit, a rebreather with a CO2 filter, pitched to the Navy (rejected) and used by the OSS, and later used by the US military from the 1950s to the 1980s.

segments.title: Cousteau and Gagnan's Aqua-Lung and The Silent World
segments.summary: Jacques Cousteau and Emile Gagnan updated the demand regulator, drawing on Gagnan's wartime gas regulator, and called it the Aqua-Lung. Cousteau's film The Silent World (1956) popularized it, winning an Oscar and the Palme d'Or, and the Aqua Master regulator followed in 1958.

segments.title: Transition to dive types
segments.summary: After a break, the hosts begin describing types of diving, starting with open water diving.

segments.title: Open water, night, and drift diving
segments.summary: Open water diving is defined as having no ceiling overhead, and can occur in lakes or quarries. Night diving is described as more dangerous due to getting lost, so divers stay tethered. Drift diving uses currents to travel with less effort, and uses more oxygen only when working hard.

segments.title: Technical, wreck, and deep diving
segments.summary: Technical diving is an umbrella for advanced diving. Wreck diving on sunken ships is dangerous because of entanglement and overhead ceilings. Deep diving requires certification, with a recreational limit around 130 feet (40 meters), with deeper dives possible with experience.

segments.title: Decompression sickness and the bends
segments.summary: Decompression sickness, or the bends, is caused by nitrogen bubbles forming in the blood and tissues when ascending too fast. Divers must make decompression stops. Chuck cites a record dive by Ahmed Gabr to over 1,000 feet, taking 14 minutes down and 14 hours to decompress.

segments.title: Dive planning and altitude diving
segments.summary: Divers must plan depth and time before entering the water using tables or dive computers. Altitude diving above 1,000 feet elevation carries different decompression considerations. The hosts digress into The Firm and Red Stripe beer, and the rule against diving and flying within 24 hours.

segments.title: Cavern, cave, and ice diving
segments.summary: Cavern diving stays within the light zone with easy surface access; cave diving has no direct surface access. Ice diving occurs under thick ice, and Romu Quarry in Estonia has a sunken prison that is popular in summer.

segments.title: Scuba gear: tanks, nitrox, BCD, regulator
segments.summary: Divers breathe compressed air, not pure oxygen; nitrox (32% oxygen) allows longer dives with fewer decompression stops. The BCD controls buoyancy. The regulator has a first stage attached to the tank and a second stage mouthpiece, with a backup mouthpiece for buddy air sharing.

segments.title: Masks, fins, dive computers, wetsuits
segments.summary: Single and dual lens masks, including prescription options. Split fins are awkward. Dive computers track depth, air, and decompression status; Apple's Oceanic Plus is mentioned. Wetsuits keep divers warm, and drysuits are for water below 50 degrees Fahrenheit. Hypothermia is possible even in water near 80 degrees.

segments.title: Rebreathers
segments.summary: A rebreather recycles exhaled air by scrubbing CO2 and adding oxygen, producing no bubbles and allowing longer dives. The record for rebreather time is 145 hours.

segments.title: Certification and how to get certified
segments.summary: No law requires a license, but dive operators ask for a card. Discover Scuba is a short introductory option. Open water certification takes a few days and costs around 500 dollars, requires age 10, and has agencies such as PADI, NAUI, and SSI. Four to six open water dives are needed, and classroom, confined water, and open water stages are described.

segments.title: Scuba risks, medical conditions, and fatality statistics
segments.summary: Pre-existing heart conditions require doctor consultation. Scuba carries risk; about 100 deaths annually in North America and about 100 more internationally. Roughly 3.4 to 4.2 deaths per 100,000 divers, with most fatalities linked to being separated from or lacking a buddy, and solo diving.

segments.title: Controlled emergency swimming ascent
segments.summary: Panicked divers who hold their breath while ascending risk lung overexpansion and arterial gas embolism. The controlled emergency swimming ascent involves swimming up slowly while exhaling.

segments.title: Radiohead banter
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh joke about the Radiohead album and EP titled Bends, with Chuck clarifying the difference between the EP and full-length LP.

segments.title: Kombucha corrections from Frederick Overbey Peterson
segments.summary: A listener named Frederick corrects them: store-bought kombucha can start a batch without a SCOBY, and SCOBYs form in some vinegars such as apple cider vinegar rather than kombucha. Josh and Chuck invite listeners to email Stuff Podcasts at iHeartRadio dot com.
